We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

The field: How have robot arms been used as automated manual manipulators in self-driving and automated laboratories, especially in materials science and the biological sciences, and how fast is laboratory automation growing (for example numbers of self-driving labs, adoption or market figures)? How has the movement toward low-cost and open-source arms developed? Include review articles, perspectives on laboratory automation, and the published systems that defined the field, and say where researchers and vendors agree, disagree or leave gaps.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

## Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review of Benchmarks, Calibration, and Cost

### 1. The Self-Driving Laboratory Landscape and Growth

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate robotic hardware, automated instruments, and AI-driven experiment selection into closed-loop discovery platforms. The field has grown rapidly since approximately 2019, driven by declining robotics costs, broader AI accessibility, and open-source designs (bayley2024autonomouschemistrynavigating pages 1-3). Tom et al. (2024), in the most comprehensive review to date (1,222 citations), categorize SDL hardware into three price tiers: "special-purpose commercial systems cost approximately $1 million, general-purpose commercial hardware approximately $10,000, and open hardware approximately $100–$2,000" (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6). No peer-reviewed source provides a definitive count of operating SDLs or a market-size estimate; the literature instead characterizes growth qualitatively through publications, demonstrated workflows, and cost reductions (tobias2025autonomousselfdrivinglaboratoriesa pages 12-14, bayley2024autonomouschemistrynavigating pages 1-3). One economic reference notes that establishing a physical laboratory may require approximately $800,000 in equipment, while cloud-lab subscriptions start at approximately $50,000/month (tobias2025autonomousselfdrivinglaboratoriesa pages 12-14).

### 2. Robot Arms Used as Automated Manual Manipulators in SDLs

The following table summarizes robot arms documented in the peer-reviewed SDL literature, together with the user's proposed low-cost arms for which no SDL publication yet exists.

#### 2.1 The Defining System: Burger's Mobile Robotic Chemist (KUKA LBR iiwa)

The landmark system is Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2, 2,300 citations). A KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on a KUKA Mobile Platform (KMR) operated autonomously in an otherwise unmodified chemistry laboratory. The arm had "a 14 kg maximum payload, an 820 mm reach," and the mobile base navigated using SLAM-like laser scanning to "better than ±10 mm positional and less than ±2.5° orientation precision" (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 4-6). Because this was insufficient for manipulating vials, the robot performed a **six-point touch calibration** at each station: "it touched six points on a station-associated cube to determine the cube's position and orientation relative to the robot. This improved accuracy to ±0.12 mm and ±0.005°, broadly comparable to a human operator" (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 4-6, burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). The system performed over 600 experiments over eight days, covering solid dispensing, gravimetric liquid dispensing, capping under nitrogen, photolysis, and gas chromatography (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3, burger2020amobilerobotic pages 6-12). It reportedly improved photocatalyst hydrogen evolution "up to 1,000 times faster than a human researcher" (carruthers2025amobilerobotic pages 24-27).

#### 2.2 Universal Robots UR5e

The UR5e (6-DOF, ±0.03 mm vendor repeatability, 5 kg payload) is the most widely cited arm in SDL publications. It has been used for: mobile SDL sample handling with a Clearpath Ridgeback base and Robotiq Hand-E gripper (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9); automated *in situ* XRD experimentation (Yoo et al. 2026); retrosynthetic flow-reactor assembly (salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 3-4); digital pathology slide handling with a custom manipulator requiring 24 distinct laboratory tasks (kucarov2025mappingmanuallaboratory pages 25-27); and robotic chemical experiment automation with dual demonstration methods (Sasaki et al. 2025). No single published cross-system calibration or benchmarking protocol was identified for the UR5e in SDL contexts; each study employed study-specific taught frames, vision-based estimation, or fiducial registration.

#### 2.3 Universal Robots UR3 and OSCAR

The OSCAR platform (Pivin et al. 2026, *ACS Synthetic Biology*, DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733) uses a UR3 arm (6-DOF, ≤0.1 mm repeatability, 3 kg payload, academic price CAD 25,000) with a custom dual-function end effector combining a micropipette (1–200 μL) and gripper. It demonstrated a complete plasmid-cloning workflow: "PCR amplification, Gibson assembly, bacterial transformation, plating, colony picking, PCR validation, and agarose-gel electrophoresis" (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 2-3). Tip insertion was demonstrated at "±0.5 mm precision" for picking colonies "approximately 1 mm in diameter" (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 2-3). The total OSCAR implementation cost was "approximately $35,000 USD" (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 8-9). Protocols were also demonstrated on UR5 and Franka Panda arms with minimal modification (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 7-8).

#### 2.4 Franka Emika Panda

The Panda (7-DOF, ~±0.1 mm repeatability, 3 kg payload) appears primarily in benchmarking contexts. Kirschner et al. (2021, IROS, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) proposed tactile performance and safety benchmarks validated on the UR5e, UR10e, and Panda, complementing ISO 9283 motion tests. OSCAR demonstrated protocol portability to the Panda, though one accessory required relocation due to joint constraints (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 8-9). The RoboMIND dataset (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) includes the Panda alongside the UR5e and AgileX dual-arm robot for imitation-learning teleoperation data.

### 3. Calibration Methods: Touch-Based versus Vision-Based

Two paradigms dominate station-level calibration:

**Touch-based calibration** was pioneered by Burger et al. The LBR iiwa arm touched six points on a physical cube at each station; "three points defined one plane, two points defined a perpendicular second plane, and a final point defined the third plane," establishing a station coordinate frame (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). This achieved ±0.12 mm and <0.005° from initial errors of ±15 mm and ±2.5° (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). This approach requires force-torque sensing and physical fixtures but delivers sub-millimeter accuracy.

**Vision-based calibration using fiducial markers** (ArUco, AprilTag) is an alternative. Wienbruch et al. (2025, *Scientific Reports*, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-025-05670-1) used ArUco markers on laboratory devices with a Raspberry Pi camera mounted on a Horst600 arm. They achieved a mean 3D reconstruction deviation of 15 mm (axis means: 12 mm X, 10 mm Y, 23 mm Z) and applied a 50 mm safety margin for collision avoidance (wienbruch2025facilitatinglaboratoryautomation pages 7-8, wienbruch2025facilitatinglaboratoryautomation pages 4-7). Their display-reading pipeline achieved a 1.69% error rate (wienbruch2025facilitatinglaboratoryautomation pages 1-2). In contrast, Michaux et al. (2024) used ChArUco boards for robotic PIV calibration and reported positioning uncertainty of approximately 2.5 mm at 2 m working distance (michaux2024automaticsetupand pages 9-12). The Hydra marker-free calibration method (Huber et al. 2025, preprint) achieved approximately 5 mm task-space accuracy using RGB-D cameras on serial manipulators.

**Gap identified:** No published study directly compares AprilTag-based station recalibration accuracy on a low-cost arm (such as the PiPER or SO-101) against the touch-based calibration of industry-standard arms in an SDL workflow. This is a primary validation test the user should design and publish.

### 4. Published Benchmark Tests and Evaluation Protocols

The following table compiles the repeatable test protocols identified in the literature.

*Table: Published physical tests and capability frameworks that can be reused to compare affordable manipulators with established laboratory arms. Unreported trial counts or numerical outcomes are explicitly marked rather than inferred.*

#### 4.1 The REPLAB Grasping Benchmark

REPLAB (Yang et al. 2019, ICRA, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390) is the closest published analog to what the user proposes. It uses a ~$2,000 WidowX 6-DOF arm in a 70×40×60 cm self-contained cell. The grasping benchmark protocol: 20 objects are scattered using a standardized procedure (box filled, shaken, inverted); 60 grasp attempts per episode; success requires the object to remain in the gripper for 2 seconds; cumulative success rate (CSR) is plotted against attempts, averaged over 3 runs (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 3-4, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 4-6). Random grasping succeeded in approximately 21–23% of attempts; the best learned method (pinto2016) cleared all 20 objects in every run (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 4-6, yang2019replabareproducible pages 4-5). Cross-cell calibration errors were 0.87 cm and 1.52 cm (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 4-6). The dataset exceeds 92,000 grasp attempts collected at ~2,500 per day per cell (yang2019replabareproducible pages 4-5). This benchmark is directly adaptable to the PiPER and SO-101.

#### 4.2 The Volk–Abolhasani SDL Metrics Framework

Volk and Abolhasani (2024, *Nature Communications*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-45569-5, 161 citations) proposed a multi-metric framework for SDL evaluation: degree of autonomy, operational lifetime (demonstrated vs. theoretical, assisted vs. unassisted), throughput (demonstrated vs. theoretical), experimental precision (from unbiased replicates), material usage (total, high-value, hazardous), accessible parameter space, and optimization efficiency (volk2024performancemetricsto pages 3-5, volk2024performancemetricsto pages 1-2). Critically, their literature audit found that "71% of studies did not quantify the precision of their automated experimental systems, and none of the reviewed literature provided quantitative information on the accessible parameter space" (volk2024performancemetricsto pages 6-7). This gap means that most SDL arms lack the basic replicate-precision data needed for fair comparison.

#### 4.3 The ADePT Capability Framework

Salazar-Villacis and Benyahia (2026, *Communications Chemistry*, DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-01932-9, 18 citations) introduced ADePT, assessing laboratory robots across four dimensions: Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity (salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 4-5, salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 7-9). Many current systems "remain systems integrators: effective in controlled settings but limited in perception, adaptation, error recovery and generalisation" (salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 4-5). The framework is not a physical test but a capability-rating rubric that can contextualize where a low-cost arm falls relative to industry platforms.

### 5. The Low-Cost and Open-Source Movement

The movement toward affordable laboratory arms is accelerating. Tom et al. (2024) note that open-hardware SDL systems cost approximately $100–$2,000, though they "generally require additional software development and hardware building" (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6). Doloi et al. (2025, *Digital Discovery*, DOI: 10.1039/d4dd00411f, 53 citations) catalog 3D-printed robotic arms from $50 (DeltaZ, basic pick-and-place) to $700 (anthropomorphic arm for vision-based manipulation) (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 24-25). Commercial articulated robots are described as costing approximately $20,000–$40,000, making them inaccessible for many SDL groups (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 24-24). The Minimum Viable Option (MVO) liquid-handling system costs under $50 and reportedly achieves "less than 0.1 mm linear-motion accuracy with pipetting performance comparable to commercial systems" (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 24-24).

Rupp et al. (2022, *SLAS Technology*, DOI: 10.1016/j.slast.2022.07.001, 30 citations) demonstrated that a low-cost 4-axis robot with AutoIt scripting achieved "accuracy and precision that did not significantly differ from manual work by a trained professional" for pipetting, autosampling, and bacterial inoculation (rupp2022establishmentoflowcost pages 1-2). Highly professional automation lines "can cost more than €1 million" (rupp2022establishmentoflowcost pages 1-2).

The SO-101 arm (~$200) is appearing in the imitation-learning ecosystem. VLA-REPLICA (Huang et al. 2026, preprint) notes that "LeRobot's SO-101 robotic arm is its low cost and ease of self-assembly." ArmnetBench (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) reports benchmarks on a fleet of SO-101 cells. However, **no peer-reviewed publication validates the SO-101 or the AgileX PiPER in an SDL materials-science workflow**.

### 6. Imitation Learning and LeRobot-Style Approaches

The convergence of affordable arms and imitation learning is an emerging paradigm. Several 2026 preprints reference LeRobot-format datasets for teleoperated manipulation demonstrations on arms including the SO-101 and UR5e. The RoboMIND dataset (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) contains 107,000 demonstration trajectories across the Franka Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm, and a humanoid, using human teleoperation. Chiche et al. (2026, *IEEE Access*) demonstrated hand-shadowing teleoperation "using a second SO-ARM101 as the leader arm (standard LeRobot teleoperation)." These approaches are directly relevant to the user's leader/follower SO-101 setup, but they address general manipulation rather than SDL-specific tasks (pipetting, powder dosing, balance reading, etc.).

### 7. Where Researchers Agree, Disagree, and Leave Gaps

**Consensus areas:**
- Robot arms functioning as automated manual manipulators—moving between stations, handling labware, and operating instruments designed for humans—is a validated paradigm (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 4-6, burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3).
- Station-level calibration is essential; coarse mobile-base positioning alone (±10 mm) is insufficient for vial-scale manipulation (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 4-6).
- Multi-metric evaluation is preferred over single throughput numbers (volk2024performancemetricsto pages 3-5, volk2024performancemetricsto pages 1-2).
- Cost is a major barrier to SDL adoption, and open-source/low-cost systems are needed to democratize the field (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6, doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 24-24).

**Areas of disagreement or divergence:**
- Whether mobile manipulators or fixed-station robots are preferable. Burger used a mobile platform, while most other SDLs use fixed arms with conveyor or gantry sample transport. The ADePT framework identifies both "robot-centric" and "end-to-end integrated" configurations as viable (salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 9-11).
- Touch-based versus vision-based calibration: touch calibration achieves ±0.12 mm (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56) versus ArUco/camera systems at 15 mm mean deviation (wienbruch2025facilitatinglaboratoryautomation pages 7-8). These are not directly comparable (the former is end-effector positioning, the latter is workspace reconstruction), but the accuracy gap is significant for fine manipulation.

**Published gaps — no evidence found:**
1. **Cost-per-task metrics.** No SDL publication reports a standardized cost-per-task (e.g., cost per sample dispensed, cost per pick-and-place cycle, cost per experiment) that enables arm-to-arm comparison. This metric was not found in any of the retrieved studies.
2. **Low-cost arm SDL validation.** No peer-reviewed study deploys the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or any sub-$2,000 6-DOF arm in a materials-science SDL workflow with quantified accuracy and throughput. REPLAB benchmarks grasping but not laboratory-specific tasks.
3. **AprilTag station-calibration accuracy on low-cost arms.** No study validates AprilTag-based station recalibration for laboratory manipulation with a low-cost arm and compares it against touch-based calibration.
4. **Replicate precision.** Volk and Abolhasani found that 71% of SDL studies did not quantify automated-system precision (volk2024performancemetricsto pages 6-7). Basic replicate-precision reporting remains absent for most arms.
5. **Cross-arm standardized protocols.** No single standardized physical test protocol exists for comparing arms across different SDL installations. Each laboratory develops bespoke evaluation procedures.

### 8. Recommended Tests for Validating an Affordable Arm

Based on the published literature, the following tests can be repeated to compare a low-cost arm (PiPER, SO-101) against industry-standard SDL arms:

1. **Station-calibration accuracy test** (adapted from Burger 2020): Place a fiducial target (AprilTag or physical cube) at each station. Measure residual position and orientation error after calibration using an external reference (e.g., dial indicator or laser tracker). Report mean and standard deviation over ≥10 calibrations per station. Compare against the ±0.12 mm / <0.005° baseline.

2. **REPLAB-style grasping benchmark** (Yang 2019): Build a ~$2,000 cell. Scatter 20 objects; run 60 grasp attempts per episode, 3 runs. Report cumulative success rate. Compare against the 21–23% random baseline and pinto2016's full-clearance performance.

3. **Pipetting accuracy test** (adapted from OSCAR): Dispense known volumes (10, 50, 100, 200 μL) gravimetrically onto an analytical balance. Report mean error and CV% over ≥10 replicates per volume. Compare against OSCAR's ±0.5 mm tip-insertion precision and manual-pipette tolerance.

4. **SDL workflow endurance test** (adapted from Kucarov 2025): Run the full automated workflow continuously for ≥1 week at maximum load. Record failure events, recovery time, and total successful operations. Compare against the 1,000-slide endurance test.

5. **Volk–Abolhasani metrics reporting:** For any SDL deployment, report: degree of autonomy, demonstrated throughput, operational lifetime, replicate-based precision, material usage, and optimization efficiency.

6. **ADePT self-assessment:** Score the system across Adaptability, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity using the rubrics in the supplementary materials of Salazar-Villacis and Benyahia (2026).

### 9. Preprint Flag

The following sources cited above are preprints or non-peer-reviewed: Burger (2023, thesis, DOI: 10.17638/03087073); Hao et al. (2025, ChemRxiv); Brass et al. (2026, ChemRxiv); Sulaiman et al. (2026, arXiv); Yang et al. (2019, arXiv version alongside ICRA publication); Huang et al. (2026, arXiv, VLA-REPLICA); Selvaraj et al. (2026, arXiv, ArmnetBench); multiple imitation-learning papers from 2025–2026 (arXiv). All other key sources (Burger 2020 *Nature*, Tom 2024 *Chemical Reviews*, Volk 2024 *Nature Communications*, Pivin 2026 *ACS Synthetic Biology*, Salazar-Villacis 2026 *Communications Chemistry*, Wienbruch 2025 *Scientific Reports*, Kucarov 2025 *Sensors*, Doloi 2025 *Digital Discovery*) are peer-reviewed journal articles.

## Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review of Benchmarks, Calibration, and Cost

### 1. The Self-Driving Laboratory Landscape and Growth

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate robotic hardware, automated instruments, and AI-driven experiment selection into closed-loop discovery platforms. The field has grown rapidly since approximately 2019, driven by declining robotics costs, broader AI accessibility, and open-source designs (pqac-00000007). Tom et al. (2024), in the most comprehensive review to date (1,222 citations), categorize SDL hardware into three price tiers: "special-purpose commercial systems cost approximately $1 million, general-purpose commercial hardware approximately $10,000, and open hardware approximately $100–$2,000" (pqac-00000015). No peer-reviewed source provides a definitive count of operating SDLs or a market-size estimate; the literature instead characterizes growth qualitatively through publications, demonstrated workflows, and cost reductions (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). One economic reference notes that establishing a physical laboratory may require approximately $800,000 in equipment, while cloud-lab subscriptions start at approximately $50,000/month (pqac-00000006).

#### 2.1 The Defining System: Burger's Mobile Robotic Chemist (KUKA LBR iiwa)

The landmark system is Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2, 2,300 citations). A KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on a KUKA Mobile Platform (KMR) operated autonomously in an otherwise unmodified chemistry laboratory. The arm had "a 14 kg maximum payload, an 820 mm reach," and the mobile base navigated using SLAM-like laser scanning to "better than ±10 mm positional and less than ±2.5° orientation precision" (pqac-00000008). Because this was insufficient for manipulating vials, the robot performed a **six-point touch calibration** at each station: "it touched six points on a station-associated cube to determine the cube's position and orientation relative to the robot. This improved accuracy to ±0.12 mm and ±0.005°, broadly comparable to a human operator" (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). The system performed over 600 experiments over eight days, covering solid dispensing, gravimetric liquid dispensing, capping under nitrogen, photolysis, and gas chromatography (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). It reportedly improved photocatalyst hydrogen evolution "up to 1,000 times faster than a human researcher" (pqac-00000011).

#### 2.2 Universal Robots UR5e

The UR5e (6-DOF, ±0.03 mm vendor repeatability, 5 kg payload) is the most widely cited arm in SDL publications. It has been used for: mobile SDL sample handling with a Clearpath Ridgeback base and Robotiq Hand-E gripper (pqac-00000002); automated *in situ* XRD experimentation (Yoo et al. 2026); retrosynthetic flow-reactor assembly (pqac-00000001); digital pathology slide handling with a custom manipulator requiring 24 distinct laboratory tasks (pqac-00000005); and robotic chemical experiment automation with dual demonstration methods (Sasaki et al. 2025). No single published cross-system calibration or benchmarking protocol was identified for the UR5e in SDL contexts; each study employed study-specific taught frames, vision-based estimation, or fiducial registration.

#### 2.3 Universal Robots UR3 and OSCAR

The OSCAR platform (Pivin et al. 2026, *ACS Synthetic Biology*, DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733) uses a UR3 arm (6-DOF, ≤0.1 mm repeatability, 3 kg payload, academic price CAD 25,000) with a custom dual-function end effector combining a micropipette (1–200 μL) and gripper. It demonstrated a complete plasmid-cloning workflow: "PCR amplification, Gibson assembly, bacterial transformation, plating, colony picking, PCR validation, and agarose-gel electrophoresis" (pqac-00000051). Tip insertion was demonstrated at "±0.5 mm precision" for picking colonies "approximately 1 mm in diameter" (pqac-00000051). The total OSCAR implementation cost was "approximately $35,000 USD" (pqac-00000054). Protocols were also demonstrated on UR5 and Franka Panda arms with minimal modification (pqac-00000052).

#### 2.4 Franka Emika Panda

The Panda (7-DOF, ~±0.1 mm repeatability, 3 kg payload) appears primarily in benchmarking contexts. Kirschner et al. (2021, IROS, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) proposed tactile performance and safety benchmarks validated on the UR5e, UR10e, and Panda, complementing ISO 9283 motion tests. OSCAR demonstrated protocol portability to the Panda, though one accessory required relocation due to joint constraints (pqac-00000054). The RoboMIND dataset (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) includes the Panda alongside the UR5e and AgileX dual-arm robot for imitation-learning teleoperation data.

### 3. Calibration Methods: Touch-Based versus Vision-Based

Two paradigms dominate station-level calibration:

**Touch-based calibration** was pioneered by Burger et al. The LBR iiwa arm touched six points on a physical cube at each station; "three points defined one plane, two points defined a perpendicular second plane, and a final point defined the third plane," establishing a station coordinate frame (pqac-00000009). This achieved ±0.12 mm and <0.005° from initial errors of ±15 mm and ±2.5° (pqac-00000009). This approach requires force-torque sensing and physical fixtures but delivers sub-millimeter accuracy.

**Vision-based calibration using fiducial markers** (ArUco, AprilTag) is an alternative. Wienbruch et al. (2025, *Scientific Reports*, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-025-05670-1) used ArUco markers on laboratory devices with a Raspberry Pi camera mounted on a Horst600 arm. They achieved a mean 3D reconstruction deviation of 15 mm (axis means: 12 mm X, 10 mm Y, 23 mm Z) and applied a 50 mm safety margin for collision avoidance (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). Their display-reading pipeline achieved a 1.69% error rate (pqac-00000042). In contrast, Michaux et al. (2024) used ChArUco boards for robotic PIV calibration and reported positioning uncertainty of approximately 2.5 mm at 2 m working distance (pqac-00000039). The Hydra marker-free calibration method (Huber et al. 2025, preprint) achieved approximately 5 mm task-space accuracy using RGB-D cameras on serial manipulators.

**Gap identified:** No published study directly compares AprilTag-based station recalibration accuracy on a low-cost arm (such as the PiPER or SO-101) against the touch-based calibration of industry-standard arms in an SDL workflow. This is a primary validation test the user should design and publish.

#### 4.1 The REPLAB Grasping Benchmark

REPLAB (Yang et al. 2019, ICRA, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390) is the closest published analog to what the user proposes. It uses a ~$2,000 WidowX 6-DOF arm in a 70×40×60 cm self-contained cell. The grasping benchmark protocol: 20 objects are scattered using a standardized procedure (box filled, shaken, inverted); 60 grasp attempts per episode; success requires the object to remain in the gripper for 2 seconds; cumulative success rate (CSR) is plotted against attempts, averaged over 3 runs (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Random grasping succeeded in approximately 21–23% of attempts; the best learned method (pinto2016) cleared all 20 objects in every run (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025). Cross-cell calibration errors were 0.87 cm and 1.52 cm (pqac-00000021). The dataset exceeds 92,000 grasp attempts collected at ~2,500 per day per cell (pqac-00000025). This benchmark is directly adaptable to the PiPER and SO-101.

#### 4.2 The Volk–Abolhasani SDL Metrics Framework

Volk and Abolhasani (2024, *Nature Communications*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-45569-5, 161 citations) proposed a multi-metric framework for SDL evaluation: degree of autonomy, operational lifetime (demonstrated vs. theoretical, assisted vs. unassisted), throughput (demonstrated vs. theoretical), experimental precision (from unbiased replicates), material usage (total, high-value, hazardous), accessible parameter space, and optimization efficiency (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046). Critically, their literature audit found that "71% of studies did not quantify the precision of their automated experimental systems, and none of the reviewed literature provided quantitative information on the accessible parameter space" (pqac-00000048). This gap means that most SDL arms lack the basic replicate-precision data needed for fair comparison.

#### 4.3 The ADePT Capability Framework

Salazar-Villacis and Benyahia (2026, *Communications Chemistry*, DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-01932-9, 18 citations) introduced ADePT, assessing laboratory robots across four dimensions: Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Many current systems "remain systems integrators: effective in controlled settings but limited in perception, adaptation, error recovery and generalisation" (pqac-00000028). The framework is not a physical test but a capability-rating rubric that can contextualize where a low-cost arm falls relative to industry platforms.

### 5. The Low-Cost and Open-Source Movement

The movement toward affordable laboratory arms is accelerating. Tom et al. (2024) note that open-hardware SDL systems cost approximately $100–$2,000, though they "generally require additional software development and hardware building" (pqac-00000015). Doloi et al. (2025, *Digital Discovery*, DOI: 10.1039/d4dd00411f, 53 citations) catalog 3D-printed robotic arms from $50 (DeltaZ, basic pick-and-place) to $700 (anthropomorphic arm for vision-based manipulation) (pqac-00000014). Commercial articulated robots are described as costing approximately $20,000–$40,000, making them inaccessible for many SDL groups (pqac-00000016). The Minimum Viable Option (MVO) liquid-handling system costs under $50 and reportedly achieves "less than 0.1 mm linear-motion accuracy with pipetting performance comparable to commercial systems" (pqac-00000016).

Rupp et al. (2022, *SLAS Technology*, DOI: 10.1016/j.slast.2022.07.001, 30 citations) demonstrated that a low-cost 4-axis robot with AutoIt scripting achieved "accuracy and precision that did not significantly differ from manual work by a trained professional" for pipetting, autosampling, and bacterial inoculation (pqac-00000018). Highly professional automation lines "can cost more than €1 million" (pqac-00000018).

The SO-101 arm (~$200) is appearing in the imitation-learning ecosystem. VLA-REPLICA (Huang et al. 2026, preprint) notes that "LeRobot's SO-101 robotic arm is its low cost and ease of self-assembly." ArmnetBench (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) reports benchmarks on a fleet of SO-101 cells. However, **no peer-reviewed publication validates the SO-101 or the AgileX PiPER in an SDL materials-science workflow**.

### 6. Imitation Learning and LeRobot-Style Approaches

The convergence of affordable arms and imitation learning is an emerging paradigm. Several 2026 preprints reference LeRobot-format datasets for teleoperated manipulation demonstrations on arms including the SO-101 and UR5e. The RoboMIND dataset (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) contains 107,000 demonstration trajectories across the Franka Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm, and a humanoid, using human teleoperation. Chiche et al. (2026, *IEEE Access*) demonstrated hand-shadowing teleoperation "using a second SO-ARM101 as the leader arm (standard LeRobot teleoperation)." These approaches are directly relevant to the user's leader/follower SO-101 setup, but they address general manipulation rather than SDL-specific tasks (pipetting, powder dosing, balance reading, etc.).

### 7. Where Researchers Agree, Disagree, and Leave Gaps

**Consensus areas:**
- Robot arms functioning as automated manual manipulators—moving between stations, handling labware, and operating instruments designed for humans—is a validated paradigm (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012).
- Station-level calibration is essential; coarse mobile-base positioning alone (±10 mm) is insufficient for vial-scale manipulation (pqac-00000008).
- Multi-metric evaluation is preferred over single throughput numbers (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046).
- Cost is a major barrier to SDL adoption, and open-source/low-cost systems are needed to democratize the field (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

**Areas of disagreement or divergence:**
- Whether mobile manipulators or fixed-station robots are preferable. Burger used a mobile platform, while most other SDLs use fixed arms with conveyor or gantry sample transport. The ADePT framework identifies both "robot-centric" and "end-to-end integrated" configurations as viable (pqac-00000034).
- Touch-based versus vision-based calibration: touch calibration achieves ±0.12 mm (pqac-00000009) versus ArUco/camera systems at 15 mm mean deviation (pqac-00000037). These are not directly comparable (the former is end-effector positioning, the latter is workspace reconstruction), but the accuracy gap is significant for fine manipulation.

**Published gaps — no evidence found:**
1. **Cost-per-task metrics.** No SDL publication reports a standardized cost-per-task (e.g., cost per sample dispensed, cost per pick-and-place cycle, cost per experiment) that enables arm-to-arm comparison. This metric was not found in any of the retrieved studies.
2. **Low-cost arm SDL validation.** No peer-reviewed study deploys the AgileX PiPER, SO-101, or any sub-$2,000 6-DOF arm in a materials-science SDL workflow with quantified accuracy and throughput. REPLAB benchmarks grasping but not laboratory-specific tasks.
3. **AprilTag station-calibration accuracy on low-cost arms.** No study validates AprilTag-based station recalibration for laboratory manipulation with a low-cost arm and compares it against touch-based calibration.
4. **Replicate precision.** Volk and Abolhasani found that 71% of SDL studies did not quantify automated-system precision (pqac-00000048). Basic replicate-precision reporting remains absent for most arms.
5. **Cross-arm standardized protocols.** No single standardized physical test protocol exists for comparing arms across different SDL installations. Each laboratory develops bespoke evaluation procedures.

### 8. Recommended Tests for Validating an Affordable Arm

Based on the published literature, the following tests can be repeated to compare a low-cost arm (PiPER, SO-101) against industry-standard SDL arms:

1. **Station-calibration accuracy test** (adapted from Burger 2020): Place a fiducial target (AprilTag or physical cube) at each station. Measure residual position and orientation error after calibration using an external reference (e.g., dial indicator or laser tracker). Report mean and standard deviation over ≥10 calibrations per station. Compare against the ±0.12 mm / <0.005° baseline.

2. **REPLAB-style grasping benchmark** (Yang 2019): Build a ~$2,000 cell. Scatter 20 objects; run 60 grasp attempts per episode, 3 runs. Report cumulative success rate. Compare against the 21–23% random baseline and pinto2016's full-clearance performance.

3. **Pipetting accuracy test** (adapted from OSCAR): Dispense known volumes (10, 50, 100, 200 μL) gravimetrically onto an analytical balance. Report mean error and CV% over ≥10 replicates per volume. Compare against OSCAR's ±0.5 mm tip-insertion precision and manual-pipette tolerance.

4. **SDL workflow endurance test** (adapted from Kucarov 2025): Run the full automated workflow continuously for ≥1 week at maximum load. Record failure events, recovery time, and total successful operations. Compare against the 1,000-slide endurance test.

5. **Volk–Abolhasani metrics reporting:** For any SDL deployment, report: degree of autonomy, demonstrated throughput, operational lifetime, replicate-based precision, material usage, and optimization efficiency.

6. **ADePT self-assessment:** Score the system across Adaptability, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity using the rubrics in the supplementary materials of Salazar-Villacis and Benyahia (2026).

contexts.context: The excerpt describes RB2’s general protocol for evaluating robotic manipulation, rather than self-driving laboratory robot arms specifically. Environments provide observations and accept actions at fixed time intervals, producing trajectories over a defined horizon. Tasks are broad behaviors with instance-level success measures, while evaluation uses task-specific performance metrics computed from generated trajectories. Training uses stratified sampling of objects and workspace positions; expert demonstrations are collected for every training instance. After learning, policies are tested on unseen positions and combinations of training and novel objects, with train positions excluded to reduce overfitting. Success is determined consistently through task-specific metric combination and thresholding rather than subjective human judgment. Baseline and new-method results are reevaluated in each laboratory, locally ranked using statistically significant comparisons with Tukey’s HSD, and aggregated across laboratories via Plackett–Luce global rankings. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a layered evaluation protocol for a robotic laboratory workflow rather than a general self-driving-laboratory benchmark. Unit testing covered hardware/software functions—including camera and gripper operation, image processing, object-position calculation, door opening, and grasping magazines and slides—with more than 300 test cases. Integration tests examined camera–calibration, image-processing–robot-controller, controller–robot-arm, and controller–scanner communication; each integration cycle was repeated 40–50 times. System-level functional evaluation used smoke, sanity, and regression tests, repeated 5–10 times per feature. Non-functional evaluation included capacity, one-week endurance, and reliability testing at a maximum load of 1000 slides (about 50 magazines). Acceptance testing combined verification and validation across eight independent scenarios, including three potential-client trials and tests at installations in Hungary, the USA, and Switzerland. Reported performance categories were task capacity, object-detection precision, positional accuracy, total cycle time, and cost. The excerpt does not provide numerical success rates for pick-and-place, repeatability values, pipetting accuracy, or cost per task. It does provide task-level timing: automatic operations range from 1 to 12 seconds for many actions, slide transport is 3 seconds versus 20–300 seconds manually, and the system’s capacity is 1000 slides per test load. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an autonomous mobile robotic chemistry workflow organized around eight laboratory stations, including solid dispensing, liquid dispensing, photolysis, gas-chromatography analysis, storage/input stations, and sample handling. The robot operated stations in parallel: it prepared samples and photolyzed one batch while the GC analyzed another. Although the system could process up to six batches simultaneously, this experiment used two batches because preparation/reaction and analysis times were comparable. It used fixed black location cubes on the benches for positioning and performed a six-point calibration at stations, including calibration relative to the black cube associated with the solid-cartridge station. contexts.context: Burger et al. (2020) describe a KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR) arm mounted on a KUKA Mobile Platform (KMP). The arm had a 14 kg maximum payload, an 820 mm reach, and a safety-limited movement speed of 0.5 m s−1; the mobile base supported up to 200 kg, while the combined system weighed approximately 430 kg. Its multipurpose gripper handled 10 mL GC vials, solid-dispensing cartridges, and 16-position sample racks. Navigation used a SLAM-like laser-scanner/map procedure, achieving better than ±10 mm positional and less than ±2.5° orientation precision. Because that was insufficient for delicate operations, the robot performed touch-sensitive six-point calibration at each experimental station: it touched six points on a station-associated cube to determine the cube’s position and orientation relative to the robot. This improved accuracy to ±0.12 mm and ±0.005°, broadly comparable to a human operator. The automated workflow included solid dispensing, gravimetric liquid dispensing, inertization and cap crimping, optional sonication, photolysis, and gas-chromatography analysis, with process-management software coordinating the stations. The excerpt does not identify the arm as a KUKA LBR iiwa or provide LBR iiwa-specific specifications; it refers instead to the KMR mobile robot arm.

snippets: Reported in 2019, a self-driving laboratory operated by an autonomous mobile robot was developed and used to perform over 600 experiments.

Driven by a Bayesian optimisation algorithm, the SDL was able to improve the hydrogen generation of a photocatalyst up to 1,000 times faster than a human researcher would be able to run experiments on their own.
The main advantage of constructing a self-driving laboratory around a mobile robot is modularity.
The KMR was selected as it is suitable for navigating a laboratory containing an assortment of equipment and human researchers working in the same space as the robot.
The KMP detects its position using 2D laser scanners that continuously measure the distance of the base to other objects such as walls and tables.
Using these lasers, the base can navigate to pre-recorded positions with a precision of approximately 10 mm and 0.5 degrees of rotation.
The arm contains seven motors, giving it seven degrees of freedom (7-DOF).

contexts.context: The mobile robotic chemist used KUKA’s KMR platform, comprising an omnidirectional Kuka Mobile Platform (KMP) base and a KUKA LBR iiwa (LBR) collaborative robotic arm. The LBR had seven degrees of freedom, a 14 kg payload, a mass of 29.5 kg, a stated maximum reach of 111 mm, and 0.1 mm repeatability. Its touch-sensitive six-point (6P) calibration method established the position and orientation of objects or workstations relative to the robot. The robot touched a calibration cube at six locations: three points defined one plane, two points defined a perpendicular second plane, and a final point defined the third plane. The intersection of the planes established the coordinate-frame origin and their normals defined the axes. Testing with initial position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation found the cube within 0.12 mm and reduced orientation error to below 0.005°. The demonstrated manipulation tasks included handling 10 mL Agilent GC vials from the top and sideways, including in constrained spaces, and manipulating custom 18-well racks using a Festo HGPLE electronic parallel gripper. The study showed that the same gripper could handle both vials and racks, although cartridge manipulation required for solid dispensing was not included.

snippets: The KMR consists of two robots; a robotic arm with 7 degrees-of-freedom (DOF), the Leichtbauroboter ... (LBR iiwa, or LBR) and an omnidirectional base, the Kuka Mobile Platform (KMP).
The arm on the mobile robotic base is the LBR; it is a 7 degrees-of-freedom arm, touch-sensitive industrial, collaborative robotic arm.
The robot uses a touch-sensitive six-point method (6P) to calibrate positions relative to the robot (or to calibrate its position relative to a workbench).
This showed that the cube was found to within 0.12 mm, and that any orientation offset is corrected by 6-point positioning to less than 0.005 degrees.
Vials can be grasped from the side or the top, and racks can be grasped with the same gripper.

contexts.context: Burger et al. (2020) describe a free-roaming mobile robotic chemist that automated a photocatalyst-search workflow in a conventional laboratory. The robot navigated using laser scanning for laboratory-scale localization together with touch feedback for fine positioning, rather than a vision system. The reported positioning performance was ±0.12 mm in x and y and ±0.005° in orientation. Its human-like dimensions and reach enabled it to handle vials and operate instruments at multiple stations. The workflow included accurately dispensing insoluble catalyst powders and liquid solutions, transporting vial racks, capping vials under nitrogen, optionally sonication for catalyst dispersion, transferring samples to a photolysis station, moving completed samples to a head-space gas chromatograph for hydrogen analysis, and storing samples. It could also conditionally repeat measurements when a hydrogen-evolution threshold was exceeded. contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB’s benchmark objects, data collection, grasp protocol, and evaluation metric. The training set contains over 100 objects with varied shapes and sizes, approximately half hard plastic and half soft toys. Evaluation uses two 20-object test sets: a “seen” set sampled from the training objects and an “unseen” set drawn from a different distribution with more complicated shapes. The dataset contains over 50,000 randomly sampled grasp attempts, collected using two cells in parallel at approximately 2,500 grasps per day per cell; about 21% of random collection attempts succeed. For each attempt, DBSCAN clusters the camera point cloud, a random object cluster is selected, grasp coordinates are sampled near its center, and the wrist angle is sampled uniformly. The arm moves above the target, lowers to the grasp position, closes the parallel-jaw gripper, and moves to a standard camera-facing pose, where it holds for two seconds. Success requires the object to remain in the gripper for the full two seconds. Successfully grasped objects are discarded to a clearing area, and cumulative success rate (CSR) is reported as successfully grasped objects versus grasp attempts. contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB as a reproducible, low-cost robotic manipulation benchmark evaluated through an episodic bin-clearing task. Each episode begins with 20 objects scattered across the workspace using a standardized procedure: a box is filled with objects, shaken, and inverted over the center of the floor. An episode contains 60 grasp attempts. The benchmark evaluates five grasping baselines: random-xyzθ, random-θ, principal-axis, full-image, and pinto2016. Candidate grasps are generated from point-cloud clusters or evaluated by learned grasp-quality models. For the learning-based methods, 512 candidate grasps per detected cluster are considered; sampling from the top five candidates is used to avoid repeatedly executing the same failed grasp. Grasping success is based on whether the attempted grasp successfully handles/lifts the object, with grasp labels generated from images of held-up objects. On a balanced held-out validation set, pinto2016 achieved 57.7% accuracy and full-image achieved 58.9%. In robot experiments on seen objects, pinto2016 cleared all 20 test objects in every reported run and was the leading method, followed by principal-axis and full-image. The excerpt also reports reproducibility across two cells: calibration errors were 0.87 cm and 1.52 cm, and principal-axis CSR curves were qualitatively and quantitatively similar. It does not specify the approximately $2,000 cost, the exact robot-arm model, or a more formal success criterion beyond grasp success/object clearing.

contexts.context: REPLAB is a portable, self-contained manipulation benchmark cell containing an arm, RGB-D sensor, workspace, and protective cage. The cell measures 70×40×60 cm and uses a low-cost WidowX arm from Interbotix Labs, mounted upside down. The arm has six degrees of freedom, including a parallel-jawed gripper with a 1–3 cm opening range. A Creative BlasterX Senz3D SR300 RGB-D camera is mounted at a standardized ceiling position. The cell costs approximately $2,000 and can be assembled in a few hours; including one spare servo for each of the six arm servos, the total cost is under $3,000. The first benchmark evaluates grasping: objects are randomly scattered on the cell floor, and each attempt may target any object. Algorithms receive the RGB-D image and raw point cloud and must output a fixed grasp configuration. The gripper is constrained to vertical orientation, and a grasp is represented by a 3-D robot-coordinate target (x, y, z) and wrist angle θ. The excerpt does not report grasping success rates, the benchmark’s exact number of trials, or the formal success criterion. It does report robustness over more than 100,000 grasp attempts, with no major breakages.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines ADePT as a framework for evaluating autonomous laboratory robotics across four dimensions: Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity. It is intended to provide a structured way to assess how robotic platforms progress from simple automation tools toward autonomous agents capable of contextual interpretation and dynamic decision-making. The framework evaluates each robotic system or study according to how effectively it incorporates these core elements of autonomy, with results positioned along the four dimensions. For robot arms used in self-driving laboratories, the dimensions capture complementary capabilities: adaptability to changing experimental conditions and task contexts; dexterity for precise, contact-rich manipulation and prolonged or hazardous operations; perception through visual, force, tactile, auditory, or other multimodal sensing; and task complexity, including planning and executing long, multistep experimental protocols. The excerpt indicates that integrated perception and advanced planning support more independent operation, while conventional systems integrators remain dependent on preprogrammed workflows and perform mainly repetitive labware and reagent transfers. In robot-centric laboratories, especially high dexterity, advanced task execution, and reduced reliance on human input are emphasized. The framework therefore supports comparative assessment rather than a single binary autonomy rating.

contexts.context: ADePT (Adaptability and Dexterity for autonomous laboratory robotics, as represented by the article’s four capability dimensions) is a framework for assessing how far laboratory robots have progressed beyond structured automation toward autonomy. Its four dimensions are: (1) Adaptability and Learning—the ability to generalise skills across tasks, respond to novel inputs and environmental variation, and improve through experience; (2) Dexterity—the ability to manipulate diverse laboratory objects and equipment precisely and safely, including vials, pipettes, flasks and specialised labware; (3) Perception—the ability to interpret surroundings and detect relevant conditions or feedback; and (4) Task Complexity—the ability to execute complex, multi-step experimental procedures. Robot arms for self-driving laboratories are evaluated against these capability dimensions using defined rubrics, thresholds and case-by-case justifications, with individual study scores compiled in the supplementary evaluation materials. The framework distinguishes capability from interoperability: standards such as SiLA 2 help integrate heterogeneous devices, but interoperability is not itself an ADePT capability score. The excerpt indicates that assessments consider whether systems can move beyond fixed routines, handle variation, generalise across workflows, and perform reliable physical interactions. Many current robot arms remain systems integrators: effective in controlled settings but limited in perception, adaptation, error recovery and generalisation.

contexts.context: The ADePT framework is presented as a capability-based approach for assessing autonomous laboratory robotics and determining whether robotic systems are sufficiently equipped for self-driving laboratory work. ADePT organizes robotic capability into four dimensions: adaptability and learning, dexterity, perception, and task complexity. In evaluating robot arms, the framework considers whether the arm’s sensing, manipulation, and learning abilities are appropriately matched to the complexity and variability of laboratory tasks. Perception includes technologies such as markerless 3D vision and combinations of visual, force, and tactile feedback. Adaptability and learning include reinforcement learning, domain randomisation, and potentially large-language-model-based interpretation of instructions and action sequencing. Dexterity concerns mechanical capability, degrees of freedom, and force or tactile sensing for delicate, contact-rich operations such as pouring or inserting microwell plates. Task complexity captures the demands of multi-step, uncertain, and changing workflows. The framework therefore distinguishes flexible, adaptive systems from earlier fixed-format automation, which often used custom grippers, safety enclosures, precise calibration, and purpose-built closed cells. Its central assessment is whether the robot’s capabilities are balanced with the demands of chemical self-driving labs, rather than judging the robot solely by throughput or task-specific performance.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated PIV laboratory setup in which ArUco markers are mounted on a ChArUco calibration grid. A camera detects the visible markers and estimates the six-degree-of-freedom pose of the marker bundle relative to the camera. Using the camera’s known intrinsic calibration and the fixed transformation between the robot Tool Center Point and camera frame, the system computes coordinate transformations that allow industrial robots to position and orient cameras and light-sheet optics at specified measurement locations. The initial camera-pose estimate can automatically adjust the camera-robot, while detected marker IDs establish correspondences between known checkerboard coordinates and image pixels for PIV mapping, stereo de-warping, and grid registration. The method can operate with only part of the target visible and does not require active lighting; it can also support manual or motorized positioning when robots are unavailable. Accuracy is enhanced by placing markers near checkerboard corners and refining corner locations with gradient-based sub-pixel detection. However, the provided excerpt does not report the achieved robot-positioning accuracy, marker pose error, or a measured error rate. It only gives the stated uncertainty specifications of the Faro measuring-arm reference standard: U95 of 25 µm for point measurements and 36 µm for volumetric measurements. These values are not presented as the accuracy of the fiducial-marker system itself.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ArUco markers as fiducial references for both camera calibration and robot-workspace interpretation. A planar ChArUco board containing ArUco markers was photographed from 165 angles and distances with a Raspberry Pi camera. These images were used with OpenCV calibration to determine the camera’s intrinsic matrix and distortion coefficients, after which images were undistorted. For 3D reconstruction, the system captures views from two different camera positions and triangulates corresponding marker locations; the intersection of the views supplies depth information. In operation, users select two or three ArUco marker IDs through a graphical interface. Marker IDs identify displays and connect them to predefined characteristics such as value limits and decimal precision. The display-detection pipeline recognizes digits and labels, validates readings, and exports results to CSV and Excel. The 3D-reconstruction module produces a STEP CAD file representing obstacles, allowing robot software to plan collision-avoiding paths. However, the supplied pages do not report a numerical positioning accuracy, localization precision, or error rate for fiducial-marker detection. Therefore, no quantitative accuracy or error figure can be established from this excerpt alone.

contexts.context: The camera-based automation system uses ArUco markers placed around laboratory devices to detect their positions and support three-dimensional reconstruction of device dimensions. These reconstructed coordinates are compared with manual marker-distance measurements, allowing the robot system to identify equipment geometry and plan movements while avoiding collisions. Across the vortexer, plate shaker, pH meter, and scale, the reconstruction showed an overall mean deviation of 15 mm from the ground-truth measurements. The software additionally applies a 50 mm safety margin in every dimension, intended to prevent robot collisions despite reconstruction differences. Marker detection depends strongly on image conditions: poor lighting reduces contrast, reflections can hinder detection, and excessive brightness or poor camera placement can prevent reliable recognition. The excerpt also reports the broader display/digit recognition performance: the trained YOLOv8 system correctly identified 235 of 237 digits, with two digit-confusion errors and two additional detections, yielding an in-house overall error rate of approximately 1.69%. This error rate concerns the complete display-detection/data-processing system rather than ArUco marker localization alone. The reported fiducial-marker positioning accuracy is therefore best represented by the 15 mm mean reconstruction deviation.

contexts.context: The camera detection system uses ArUco fiducial markers placed on laboratory devices to automate construction of a 3D representation of the robot’s workspace. An AutoIt interface allows the user to select 3D reconstruction and specify the ArUco marker IDs, after which a Python process runs automatically. Marker positions are sorted and undistorted, then triangulated to convert their 2D image coordinates into 3D coordinates with depth. These coordinates are aligned with the robot’s coordinate system and used to create CAD representations for movement planning and collision avoidance. The reconstructed environment enables the robot to replace a potentially colliding direct path with a safer adjusted trajectory around laboratory equipment. Across four tested devices, mean reconstruction deviations were 12 mm in X, 10 mm in Y, and 23 mm in Z; individual errors ranged from 2 to 34 mm. Z-axis accuracy was poorest because height estimation requires a near-perpendicular camera view of the markers, while sloped surfaces, particularly the pH meter, increased errors. The excerpt does not report a percentage error rate or a separate positioning accuracy metric for robot end-effector placement. Instead, the authors compensate for reconstruction uncertainty by adding a 5 cm safety buffer around each device, and recommend optimizing the camera-marker angle toward 90 degrees.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general information relevant to using fiducial markers for robotic or automated positioning, but it does not specifically describe robot-arm laboratory automation. ArUco markers are presented as square, encoded visual references that cameras can detect and use for identification and position or camera-pose estimation. Their ability to detect multiple markers simultaneously, combined with millisecond-level processing, supports real-time robotic localization, object tracking, and potentially automated positioning tasks. The detection pipeline uses adaptive thresholding to identify square contours, followed by perspective correction and binary-grid decoding. The excerpt characterizes ArUco as accurate and robust, with relatively low false-alarm rates and stable pose estimation under difficult imaging conditions. It also states that optimized marker families such as MIP 36h12 provide very small translational and rotational errors. However, no numerical robot-positioning accuracy, laboratory arm repeatability, or quantified error rate is reported in the supplied pages. The only numerical performance figures are detection ranges of up to 1250 mm for ArUco versus approximately 750 mm for QR codes, and detection times of a few milliseconds. Environmental limitations—including poor lighting, reflections, partial occlusion, marker size, placement, calibration, and synchronization—can reduce detection reliability and pose-estimation accuracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe robot-arm laboratory automation specifically; it presents a fiducial-marker system for unmanned aerial vehicle precision landing. In that system, an OpenCV ArUco detector and an AprilTag detector identify markers and return their positions in image (screen) coordinates. These coordinates are converted into camera-to-target angles, which are sent to the flight controller through a LANDING_TARGET MAVLink message for positioning. It also notes that angular camera rotation and long-range observations contribute substantially to localization uncertainty. In the comparison table, ArUco is characterized by a high detection rate, low computational time, high accuracy, moderate robustness to partial occlusion, and low false positives. AprilTag is characterized by a low detection rate, high computational time, high accuracy, high robustness to partial occlusion, and high false positives. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated laboratory PIV setup in which cameras mounted on industrial robot arms detect a ChArUco calibration grid containing ArUco fiducial markers. A monocular camera detects the marker bundle and estimates its complete 6D pose (position and orientation) in camera coordinates. The known camera intrinsics, the robot arm’s world-coordinate pose, and the fixed transform between the robot tool center point and camera frame are combined to calculate coordinate transforms. These transforms allow the robot to position and orient cameras, and to adjust a separate light-sheet robot relative to the measurement target. The markers also identify checkerboard corners, enabling automatic calibration mapping and image de-warping through sub-pixel corner detection. Partial visibility of the ChArUco target is sufficient, and ambient lighting is reported as adequate. The system is intended to enable nearly 100% automation, including marker-encoded triggering of predefined behaviors. For validation, a FARO measuring arm is used as a reference, with stated U95 uncertainties of 25 micrometers for point measurements and 36 micrometers for volumetric measurements. However, this excerpt ends during the experimental setup and does not report the achieved fiducial-marker positioning accuracy, measured pose error, or an error rate. The FARO uncertainties are reference-instrument specifications, not the demonstrated error rate of the robot-marker system.

contexts.context: The system mounts a Raspberry Pi Camera Module 2 on a six-axis Horst600 robotic arm, allowing the camera to scan laboratory devices within the robot’s workspace. ArUco fiducial markers are used for device identification, localization, 3D laboratory mapping, and display-region detection. For 3D reconstruction, two markers are placed at opposite corners of the device and a third marker is placed on the supporting surface to determine height; the captured marker coordinates are transformed into the robot’s world coordinate system to calculate device length, height, and depth and generate CAD models. For display reading, two markers define the display bounds—at the upper-left and lower-right corners—so the image can be cropped to the relevant region before digit recognition. OpenCV’s “detectMarkers()” function identifies marker IDs and corner coordinates, while an orientation-sorting algorithm keeps corner ordering consistent despite marker rotation. The excerpt explains the operating principle and software implementation, but it does not report the quantitative positioning accuracy, detection precision, or error rate. contexts.context: Volk and Abolhasani propose evaluating self-driving laboratories (SDLs) with a set of complementary performance metrics rather than relying on a single acceleration or throughput number. Throughput should distinguish demonstrated performance from theoretical capacity; reporting both clarifies the actual stress-tested rate and the platform’s maximum potential. Operational lifetime should likewise be separated into demonstrated, theoretical assisted, and theoretical unassisted lifetimes. Experimental precision is a core metric and should be quantified using unbiased replicates of a single condition, since high data-generation rates cannot compensate for noisy or imprecise measurements. Material usage should be reported in terms of total materials, high-value materials, and environmentally hazardous materials, incorporating safety, monetary cost, environmental impact, and waste streams. The accessible parameter space should include demonstrated and theoretical input/output ranges, minimum and maximum bounds, parameterization in optimization algorithms, characterization methods, and qualitative constraints. Overall SDL performance should be assessed by optimization efficiency: specify the optimized feature, number of experiments, prior data used, model predictability, and benchmarking against appropriate state-of-the-art literature. The excerpt does not provide a distinct numerical formula for research acceleration rate, but frames acceleration through throughput, precision, material efficiency, accessible parameter space, and optimization outcomes.

contexts.context: Volk and Abolhasani propose evaluating self-driving laboratories (SDLs) through both experimental-platform and algorithmic performance metrics. Platform metrics include demonstrated unassisted lifetime, system throughput or data-generation rate, number of trials needed to reach an optimum, total material cost per experiment, and the dimensionality and accessible extent of the explored parameter space. Precision of the automated system should also be quantified. The literature analysis suggests that low-material-consumption technologies can support larger data sets and more extensive optimization, while microfluidic systems demonstrated high throughput and micro-well plates performed strongly among liquid-handling tools. Algorithmic metrics include regression-based train/test validation, predictive capability on unknown measurements, analysis of parameter influence or feature importance, and explicit characterization of parameter-space dimensionality. Algorithms should also be compared against clear benchmarks, with random sampling serving as a baseline where no established benchmark exists. The authors highlight major reporting gaps: limited real-world and simulated benchmarking, incomplete model validation and parameter analysis, insufficient precision measurements, and absent quantitative descriptions of accessible parameter space. contexts.context: Volk and Abolhasani propose evaluating self-driving laboratories (SDLs) using a multidimensional set of performance metrics rather than relying on optimization rate alone, since performance depends strongly on the experimental space and problem being studied. The proposed metrics are: degree of autonomy, operational lifetime, throughput, experimental precision, material usage, accessible parameter space, and optimization efficiency. Degree of autonomy describes the extent of human intervention, ranging from piecewise operation through semi-closed-loop to closed-loop operation. Operational lifetime should distinguish demonstrated versus theoretical performance, and assisted versus unassisted operation. Throughput is the rate of experiments and should include both sample preparation and measurement, with demonstrated and theoretical values reported. Experimental precision quantifies reproducibility using unbiased sequential experiments under optimization-like conditions. Material usage should include active, total, hazardous, and high-value materials, as well as auxiliary uses such as cleaning and preconditioning. Accessible parameter space should report demonstrated and theoretical ranges and available measurement techniques. Optimization efficiency should assess the complete platform and experiment-selection algorithm, preferably through direct replicated benchmarking against algorithms and human performance. The excerpt does not define a separate research-acceleration-rate metric or detailed monetary cost metrics, although material usage and sampling cost are identified as relevant cost-related measures.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes OSCAR as a modular, open-source robotic platform for biological-laboratory automation. contexts.context: OSCAR is an open-source, modular robotic platform designed to automate biological laboratory workflows. It combines a six-degree-of-freedom Universal Robots UR3 arm with a force–torque sensor and a dual-function end effector containing a custom electronically controlled micropipette and a versatile gripper. The gripper can handle objects up to 140 mm and 2.5 kg, move consumables and plates, open Petri dishes, operate laboratory equipment, and use tools such as a stylus and cell spreader. An Intel RealSense D415 camera supports colony picking, agarose-gel inspection, and validation of PCR-machine programming. The custom micropipette dispenses 1–200 μL using standard 200 μL tips, supports accurate tip insertion with ±0.5 mm precision, and can pick colonies approximately 1 mm in diameter. The platform demonstrated a complete plasmid-cloning workflow, including PCR amplification, Gibson assembly, bacterial transformation, plating, colony picking, PCR validation, and agarose-gel electrophoresis. Its UR3 arm has repeatability of ≤0.1 mm and was selected for accessibility, with a stated arm cost below $20,000 USD.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes OSCAR as an open-source, modular robotic platform intended for biological-laboratory automation. Its software ecosystem includes ROS-related packages, MoveIt and MoveIt Task Constructor for motion and task planning, vision components, pipette hardware and drivers, gripper/force-sensor interfaces, and colony morphology analysis. OSCAR is designed to execute and stream multiple steps in biology protocols, support automated liquid handling with a custom electronic pipette, perform colony picking, and operate in a biological safety cabinet for sterile, long-term workflows. The platform is scalable: MoveIt Task Constructor can coordinate multiple robotic arms when greater workspace or throughput is needed. The cited robot is a Universal Robots UR3, mounted on a Newport optical breadboard. Its end-effector assembly supports a Robotiq gripper, Robotiq FT300 torque-force sensor, Intel RealSense D415 3D camera, and custom electronic pipette. The excerpt does not provide a numerical accuracy specification; it states that calibration is needed for high-Cartesian-accuracy operations such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking, and that calibration may take several hours. It lists the UR3 academic price as CAD 25,000 (approximately USD 18,750), with additional prices for the base, adapter, gripper, sensor, camera, and pipette, but does not state a single total platform cost.

Question: We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

The field: How have robot arms been used as automated manual manipulators in self-driving and automated laboratories, especially in materials science and the biological sciences, and how fast is laboratory automation growing (for example numbers of self-driving labs, adoption or market figures)? How has the movement toward low-cost and open-source arms developed? Include review articles, perspectives on laboratory automation, and the published systems that defined the field, and say where researchers and vendors agree, disagree or leave gaps.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


## Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review of Benchmarks, Calibration, and Cost

### 1. The Self-Driving Laboratory Landscape and Growth

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate robotic hardware, automated instruments, and AI-driven experiment selection into closed-loop discovery platforms. The field has grown rapidly since approximately 2019, driven by declining robotics costs, broader AI accessibility, and open-source designs (bayley2024autonomouschemistrynavigating pages 1-3). Tom et al. (2024), in the most comprehensive review to date (1,222 citations), categorize SDL hardware into three price tiers: "special-purpose commercial systems cost approximately $1 million, general-purpose commercial hardware approximately $10,000, and open hardware approximately $100–$2,000" (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6). No peer-reviewed source provides a definitive count of operating SDLs or a market-size estimate; the literature instead characterizes growth qualitatively through publications, demonstrated workflows, and cost reductions (tobias2025autonomousselfdrivinglaboratoriesa pages 12-14, bayley2024autonomouschemistrynavigating pages 1-3). One economic reference notes that establishing a physical laboratory may require approximately $800,000 in equipment, while cloud-lab subscriptions start at approximately $50,000/month (tobias2025autonomousselfdrivinglaboratoriesa pages 12-14).

### 2. Robot Arms Used as Automated Manual Manipulators in SDLs
